The arithmetic reproduces: U=500 pessimistic costs ¥887-891 on Colab L4; U=1,600 needs 2.4-4.7 weeks of Kaggle or ¥1.43-2.84k on Colab; U=4,000 costs ¥3.57-7.12k on Colab or 1.4-2.7 months of Kaggle. But it ignores the live Kaggle promotion for linked Colab Pro accounts (COMPUTE-15). For ¥1,179/month, Colab Pro includes 100 CU (about 58 L4-hours at 1.71 CU/h) and raises the Kaggle quota to about 45 h/week (about 195 h/month). That is about 250 GPU-hours a month, treating T4 x2 as one L4. With it, U=4,000 at N=100 centrally (177 h) fits in about 3-4 weeks for ¥1,179. The pessimistic 353 h needs about 1.1 months even at ¥2,358 (Pro plus one 100-unit Pay As You Go pack, about 312 h/month). The promotion can end without notice, so give results both with and without it.

claims.claim: USD prices were converted at an assumed ¥150/USD planning rate that was not looked up. USD/JPY may be a candidate study market whose 2024-07-01 to 2026-10-31 prices are sealed.

checks.correction: I deliberately did not look up USD/JPY, because a current spot rate would reveal where the sealed 2024-07-01 to 2026-10-31 window ended. Express USD costs as a band, for example ¥130-170 per USD, or in USD. The conclusions do not depend on it: Colab is billed in JPY, and Modal and RunPod are overflow only.

new_findings.finding: The per-year hours cover 245 trading days. The whole window after the pretraining cutoff, 2024-07-01 to 2026-10-31, is about 853 calendar days: about 2.33 years or about 572 TSE trading days. One pass over it costs 2.33 times the per-year hours. In L4 or T4x2 hours, central (pessimistic): U=500 N=100 about 52 (103); U=1,600 N=100 about 165 (330); U=4,000 N=100 about 413 (826); U=4,000 N=10 about 41 (83). Each extra pre-registered variant (N, lookback, model size, market) multiplies the cost again.
new_findings.impact: Over the full window, U=1,600 N=100 no longer fits one month of free Kaggle (about 130 h) or ¥3,000 of Colab Pay As You Go (282 units = 3 packs = ¥3,537). The budget should be set per study, not per year.
new_findings.source: Own arithmetic: 25.99 GFLOP/path (from kronos.py and module.py) x 572 days x U x N / 4.0 TFLOPS. Window dates are from the study brief.

new_findings.finding: Colab Pro costs the same ¥1,179 a month as one 100-unit Pay As You Go pack. It also qualifies for Kaggle's experimental promotion of 15 extra GPU hours a week (30 with Pro+) on the same Kaggle hardware, and those hours do not use Colab compute units. The free 30 h/week plus the bonus 15 h/week is about 195 Kaggle GPU-hours a month. Adding about 58 L4-hours from the 100 units gives about 250 L4-equivalent hours a month for ¥1,179.
new_findings.impact: For this budget Colab Pro beats Pay As You Go. One year of U=4,000 N=100 (177 h central), or the whole window at U=1,600 N=100 (165 h), fits in about a month for ¥1,179. This assumes a T4x2 is worth about one L4 and that the promotion continues; Kaggle can end it without notice. The researcher's cost figures leave this out.
new_findings.source: https://www.kaggle.com/docs/notebooks ('[EXPERIMENTAL] Increase GPU compute with Colab Pro', rendered 2026-11-08); https://colab.research.google.com/signup

new_findings.finding: The ¥3,000/month cap covers GPU and data together. Official J-Quants API prices, tax included: Free ¥0 (two years of data, excluding the latest 12 weeks); Light ¥1,650/month (5 years); Standard ¥3,300 (10 years); Premium ¥16,500. The Free plan cannot reach the 40-bar lookback before 2024-07-01, nor the latest 12 weeks of the test window.
new_findings.impact: If the market is Japanese equities via J-Quants Light, only ¥1,350 a month is left for compute. That is one ¥1,179 purchase, preferably Colab Pro, for ¥2,829 in total. The plan of buying two Pay As You Go packs (¥2,358) is then unaffordable, so the plan becomes free Kaggle plus Colab Pro.

new_findings.finding: The T4 (Turing) does not support BF16 or TF32. NVIDIA's T4 specification lists only FP32 (8.1 TFLOPS), mixed FP16/FP32 (65 TFLOPS), INT8 and INT4. PR #289's bf16 autocast, measured only on an RTX 4090, therefore gives no tensor-core speed-up on Kaggle's T4 x2. The T4 alternative is FP16 autocast, and nobody has tested whether it matches FP32 Kronos numerically.
new_findings.impact: The plan's 'bf16' fallback for U=4,000 N=100 only works on a Colab L4. On the primary platform the options are a KV cache (PRs #393 / #192) or FP16 after validating it against FP32.

new_findings.finding: Kronos-base is on HF as NeoQuasar/Kronos-base (sha 2b554741..., MIT) with d_model 832, ff_dim 2048, 12 layers and 16 heads. My parameter count is 102,310,592, which matches its 409,264,008-byte safetensors file. With the same upstream loop at lookback 40 / horizon 12 it costs about 109.6 GFLOP per path, 4.22 times Kronos-small.
new_findings.impact: If the pre-registration chooses Kronos-base, every hour and yen figure rises by about 4.2x. For example, U=1,600 N=100 becomes about 300 L4-hours per year (central). Only U<=500 or N=10 would then fit the free tier.

new_findings.finding: Cost per path grows roughly linearly with lookback, because decoder passes = 12 x lookback + 66. Cost per path: 26.0 GFLOP at lookback 40, 37.7 at 60, 55.5 at 90, 73.7 at 120 and 261 at 400 (the README example uses lookback=400). That is 1.45x, 2.14x, 2.84x and 10x the 40-bar cost.
new_findings.impact: Any lookback above 40 in the pre-registration scales all hours by the same factor. At 400 bars even U=500 N=100 needs about 220 L4-hours per year.

new_findings.finding: Sampling calls torch.multinomial on the global random generator, with no per-row generator and no seeding anywhere in kronos.py. So the paths drawn for an instrument-day depend on how batches are composed and ordered, and on the device (CPU or CUDA, T4 or L4). The forecast is the mean of N draws, so its Monte Carlo noise falls only as 1/sqrt(N). The paper's own investment simulation uses T=0.6, top_p=0.9, N=10 (Table 6).
new_findings.impact: Results will not be bit-for-bit reproducible if work is mixed between Kaggle and Colab or re-batched. The pre-registration should fix the seed, batch layout and platform, or the code should add a generator per row. N=100 is ten times the paper's trading setting; at N=10 every universe fits the free tier per year.

new_findings.finding: The google-colab-cli skill doc warns that 'an unrecognized --gpu value silently falls back to A100'. An A100-40GB burns 5.40 compute units per hour (about ¥64/h), against 1.71 (about ¥20/h) for an L4.
new_findings.impact: A typo in a headless overflow job could use up a ¥1,179 pack of 100 units in about 18.5 hours. Pin `--gpu L4` explicitly and check `colab usage`.

new_findings.finding: Kaggle's documentation does not say whether one hour of a T4 x2 session counts as one or two hours against the weekly GPU quota.
new_findings.impact: If it counts as two, free Kaggle capacity halves, from about 130 to about 65 L4-equivalent hours a month. Read the quota counter after the calibration run before scheduling the walk-forward.

new_findings.finding: Kaggle's limited-time promotion gives Colab Pro (¥1,179/month incl. tax, 100 CU/month) and Pro+ subscribers who link their accounts 15 and 30 extra Kaggle GPU hours per week. The extra hours do not consume compute units. The offer is limited to one linked Kaggle account per subscriber and can end without notice. Colab Pro costs the same as a 100-unit Pay As You Go pack (¥1,179), so if at least 100 units a month will be used, Pay As You Go alone is strictly worse.
new_findings.impact: This is the cheapest bundle within ¥3,000: about 45 Kaggle h/week plus about 58 Colab L4-hours for ¥1,179/month. It changes U=4,000 at N=100 from 'does not fit' to about one month centrally. The recommended plan should be Colab Pro plus linked Kaggle, with Pay As You Go as overflow.
new_findings.source: https://www.kaggle.com/docs/notebooks ([EXPERIMENTAL] Increase GPU compute with Colab Pro, fetched 2026-11-08); https://colab.research.google.com/signup

new_findings.finding: Modal's Starter plan includes $30/month of free credits. At the L4 rate of $0.000222/s ($0.80/h), that is about 37 L4-hours, or about 31 hours once roughly 2 physical cores and 8 GiB of memory are billed ($0.0000131 per core-second, $0.00000222 per GiB-second). List prices are preemptible; non-preemptible costs 3x and region pinning 1.15-1.75x. Unknown: whether Starter needs a payment card, and whether Modal charges Japanese consumption tax.
new_findings.impact: Potentially another 30-37 L4-hours a month at no marginal cost, provided jobs checkpoint and survive preemption.

new_findings.finding: In Kaggle kernel-metadata.json, enable_gpu and enable_internet both default to false when omitted, so a headless `kaggle kernels push` runs on CPU with no internet unless both are set. NvidiaL4 ('GPU L4 x4') and NvidiaL4X1 ('GPU L4 x1') exist in the API, but the docs say some accelerators are competition- or admin-only, so free accounts should plan on T4 x2 only.
new_findings.impact: Prevents wasted runs. Do not plan on Kaggle L4s. The weights can come from a private Kaggle dataset, so internet can stay off.

new_findings.finding: Kaggle does not document whether a T4 x2 session uses quota at 1x or 2x per hour; this is unknown. The UI says quota covers 'all interactive and committed notebooks'. The two docs disagree on the interactive idle timeout: 20 minutes in Notebooks docs, 60 minutes in the GPU tips page.
new_findings.impact: The 30 h/week of T4 x2 assumption could halve. The planned Kaggle calibration run should also record how much quota it consumed.

new_findings.finding: On Colab, even paid plans are capped: 'In general, notebooks can run for at most 12 hours'. The backend terminates sessions when compute units run out. Only Pro+ (¥5,767, over budget) gets 24-hour continuous or background execution.
new_findings.impact: Colab overflow jobs also need date chunks under 12 h, checkpointing, and a positive unit balance.

new_findings.finding: The official Colab CLI includes `colab ssh`. However, the FAQ disallows SSH shells and remote desktops on free runtimes without a positive compute-unit balance. Free GPU allocation through the CLI is unreliable (412 / 'Allocation refused'), and `colab usage` does not show the free allowance.
new_findings.impact: On a free account, use only `colab run` or `colab exec` and do not count on GPUs. With any paid unit balance these restrictions lift.

new_findings.finding: Eligible paid Google AI plans now include a monthly Colab compute-unit allotment, applied automatically; the rollout reached Asia/Oceania on 17 September. The amounts are not published in the FAQ. Free trials do not qualify.
new_findings.impact: Anyone who already pays for an eligible Google AI plan may already hold compute units at no extra cost. Check Colab Settings > Subscription before buying.

new_findings.finding: I re-ran the laptop benchmark: 272.5 ms per path at 200 rows but 493.9 ms per path at 400 rows. The U-series CPU under sustained or contended load reaches about 50 GFLOPS effective.
new_findings.impact: A laptop-only fallback is up to 2x worse than stated (U=500 at N=100 is about 1,700 h), which reinforces the GPU-only plan.

title: Competition and short-horizon predictability across the four markets

research.topic: Phase 0: competition and documented short-horizon price/volume predictability. TSE stocks/ETFs vs OSE index futures vs retail FX vs US stocks, and which Kronos use fits each market
research.summary: Ranked by the chance that a candle-only model keeps an edge after costs: (1) TSE single stocks, cross-sectional ranking at a 5–12 trading-day horizon in liquid (TOPIX500-type) names, long-only or long-biased. (2) OSE Nikkei 225 Micro or mini-TOPIX futures, with Kronos used only for volatility forecasts that size a fixed exposure. (3) US stocks, only as monthly low-turnover ranking. (4) Retail FX direction, which is the least likely. The case for Japan: momentum is absent there, 1-month and weekly reversal is documented, and a US-trained CNN on 5-day OHLC images transferred to Japan with a gross weekly long-short Sharpe of 5.84 equal-weight and 1.30 value-weight (1993–2019). Anomalies also show no reliable decay after publication outside the US. Trading the large caps is cheap: one tick is about 1–5 bp in TOPIX500 names. On the other side of the trade: foreigners do 66% of Prime trading value, individuals 27% (about three-quarters of it on margin, contrarian) and HFTs the high-30s% of TSE value. Intraday is HFT territory: HFT is 60–65% of Nikkei 225 mini value and about 99% of OSE orders. The US has the strongest gross candle predictability but the most competition: HFT above 50% of volume, and anomaly returns fall 58% after publication. Its weekly large-cap spread (12 bp/week gross) is smaller than even institutional costs, and access through Japanese brokers costs 0.495% per side. FX majors are close to a random walk, technical-rule profits there had disappeared by the early 1990s, and Japanese retail traders are already the contrarian crowd. Kronos also gets zero volume for FX, and volatility targeting does not raise Sharpe for currencies. Avoid intraday and 1-day horizons; 5–12 days is the only zone that is workable for ranking. Single-instrument direction at IC ≈ 0.02 cannot be tested statistically (about 22,500 independent observations are needed for t = 3). Even cross-sectionally, a 12-day IC of 0.02 is unlikely to reach Newey-West t ≥ 3 in the roughly 460-day dev window. Structural changes to flag: the TSE close moved to a 15:30 closing auction on 2024-11-05, inside the dev window; a per-stock tick regime starts 2027-03-01; and a random close starts 2027-10-12.
research.findings_md:
# Phase 0: competition and short-horizon predictability in four candidate markets

As of 2026-11-08. The question: who is on the other side of the trade (official participation and HFT statistics), what the literature documents about short-horizon price and volume predictability, and where a candle-only model is most and least likely to keep an edge after costs. The model is Kronos-small in the daily setting: lookback 40 bars, horizon 12 bars.

**Sealed-window compliance.** I did not look up any prices, returns, backtests or Kronos results for 2024-07-01 to 2026-10-31. Statistics I used from that period are limited to participation shares, HFT shares, volumes and rules. Every academic sample I relied on ends in 2019 or earlier. I skipped two sources on purpose because they discuss or embed sealed-window price behaviour: a 2026 BOJ FX-market review centred on April 2025, and a JPX investment-unit distribution note.

## 1. Verdict

| Rank | Market | Kronos use that fits | Horizon | Competition (Section 2) | Documented predictability (Section 3) | Cost hurdle (Section 4) | Prior for a cost-surviving candle edge |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | TSE stocks (liquid, TOPIX500-type names) | Cross-sectional ranking; volatility forecasts are secondary | 5–12 trading days | Foreigners 66% of Prime value; individuals 27% (about three-quarters on margin, contrarian); proprietary 11%; HFT in the high-30s% of TSE value, of which about 15 points are directional | Best non-US evidence: 1-month and weekly reversal; no 12-1 momentum; a US-trained candle CNN transfers to Japan (gross weekly long-short Sharpe 5.84 equal-weight, 1.30 value-weight); no reliable decay after publication outside the US | Low in TOPIX500 names (1 tick ≈ 1–5 bp) if commission ≈ 0; high in small caps (1 tick ≈ 3–33 bp) | Highest of the four, but still low. The binding constraint is breadth: 100-share lots at ¥500k allow only a handful of names |
| 2 | OSE index futures (Nikkei 225 Micro and mini, mini-TOPIX) | Volatility forecasts that size a fixed exposure; direction only as a secondary test, and that test is underpowered | 1–12 days (volatility) | Foreigners 69–94% of brokerage volume; HFT 60–65% of Nikkei 225 mini trading value | Time-series momentum at 1–12 months (contested); intraday momentum in Japan (contested by HFTs); no robust daily direction signal | Very low (Micro ≈ 2.4 bp round trip at JPX's own 30,000 index example) | Medium for added value from sizing (risk), low for direction |
| 3 | US stocks via a Japan-licensed broker | Ranking only in a monthly, low-turnover setting; volatility sizing | ≥ 1 month | HFT estimated above 50% of volume; more than 90% of retail marketable orders internalised by six wholesalers; the most-studied market | Strongest gross candle predictability (weekly long-short Sharpe 7.15) but concentrated in small caps; in the 500 largest stocks only 0.12%/week gross at about 178% weekly turnover; anomaly returns fall 58% after publication | Highest: 0.495% per side (cap $22) at mainstream Japanese brokers, about 1% round trip on small tickets | Low; dominated by costs and competition |
| 4 | Retail FX (OTC, FFAJ dealers) | Volatility forecasts for risk control only | (none recommended) | Algorithmic interbank market; Japanese retail is the largest retail FX market and is contrarian at holding periods of a day or more | The random walk is the hardest benchmark to beat; technical-rule profits in major currencies had disappeared by the early 1990s; currency momentum is blocked by frictions; volatility targeting adds no Sharpe for FX | Low per trade (exact retail spreads unknown here) | Lowest for direction |

**Answers to the brief.**
- **Most likely:** TSE single stocks, ranked cross-sectionally over 5–12 trading days in liquid names, long-only or long-biased. Second: OSE Micro futures, with Kronos used only to forecast volatility for sizing; this needs ¥1–3M before sizing becomes granular (Section 4.3).
- **Least likely:** single-instrument FX direction. Next is short-horizon US ranking through Japanese retail brokers, where the problem is cost rather than missing predictability.
- **Horizon:** not intraday (HFT territory, and outside the pre-registered daily setting). Not 1-day either: it earns a liquidity-provision premium, at about 100% turnover per day. 5–12 days is the workable zone for ranking. For a single instrument, no horizon gives a testable direction edge at IC ≈ 0.02.

## 2. Competition: who is on the other side

### 2.1 TSE cash equities

Source: JPX 投資部門別売買状況, by value, trading participants with capital ≥ ¥3bn. Investor columns are % of brokerage trading; proprietary is % of total trading value.

| Segment, year | Proprietary | Foreigners | Individuals | Institutions |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Prime 2025 | 10.9 | 66.2 | 26.7 | 6.6 |
| Standard 2025 | 5.3 | 48.0 | 47.6 | 3.7 |
| Growth 2025 | 3.9 | 42.2 | 55.0 | 2.2 |
| Prime 2023 | 11.5 | 69.6 | 23.1 | 6.8 |

- **Margin share.** In 2025, 73.6% of individuals' Prime sales and 75.9% of their purchases were margin (信用) trades. Individual flow is short-horizon speculation.
- **Behaviour.** Domestic investors trade contrarian and foreigners chase trends. Source: RIETI DP 17-E-003, which cites Kamesaka et al. (2003) and Bae et al. (2008) and adds its own weekly TSE data.
- **HFT is not a JPX category.** Foreign HFTs appear mostly under "foreigners".

### 2.2 OSE index futures

Source: JPX 投資部門別取引状況, by volume, annual. Proprietary is % of total; the other columns are % of brokerage.

| Product, 2025 | Proprietary | Foreigners | Individuals | Institutions |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nikkei 225 Futures | 11.0 | 83.8 | 8.7 | 7.5 |
| Nikkei 225 mini | 1.7 | 75.0 | 23.7 | 1.2 |
| Nikkei 225 Micro | 0.0 | 69.3 | 30.4 | 0.3 |
| TOPIX Futures | 16.6 | 93.6 | 0.8 | 5.6 |
| mini-TOPIX | 3.0 | 90.4 | 7.9 | 1.8 |
| TSE Growth 250 Futures | 15.7 | 59.8 | 33.4 | 6.8 |

The 2023 structure was similar:
- Nikkei 225 Futures: foreigners 82.8, individuals 10.1.
- Nikkei 225 mini: foreigners 77.6, individuals 21.7.
- Nikkei 225 Micro (trading from 2023-05-29): foreigners 63.4, individuals 36.3.
- TOPIX Futures: foreigners 91.4, individuals 0.7.

### 2.3 HFT footprint

Source: FSA 高速取引行為の動向, published 2026-09, data January 2025 to June 2026.

| Venue | HFT share of trading value | HFT value by strategy (market-making / arbitrage / directional / other) | HFT share of orders | HFT share of executions |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TSE-listed issues (4,437 at end-June 2026) | Mainly high 30s % | ~15 / 10 / 40 / 35 | ~80% of new orders, ~90% of cancels; colocation-routed HFT ~85% of all orders | ~40% |
| OSE derivatives, all products | 35–50% | ~25 / 10 / 30 / 35 | ~99% of new orders and cancels | ~65% |
| Nikkei 225 mini | 60–65% | | | |
| Nikkei 225 Futures | 40–60% | | | |
| TOPIX Futures | 25–60% | | | |

- 52 HFT firms were registered at end-June 2026.
- My arithmetic: directional HFT is about 14–16% of TSE trading value (0.35–0.39 × 0.40) and about 10–15% of OSE value (0.35–0.50 × 0.30).
- In 2010 the arrowhead platform made algorithmic trading cheaper, which narrowed TSE spreads and deepened the book (Moriyasu, Wee & Yu, 2018).

### 2.4 Retail FX in Japan

- **Scale.**
  - 46 FFAJ dealers handled about ¥1,227 trillion of OTC retail FX volume in September 2026; open interest was about ¥11.7 trillion.
  - Japan accounted for 36% of global retail spot FX in BIS 2013.
  - Japanese retail margin volume exceeded Tokyo interbank spot volume from 2013: 1.5× in 2017 and 1.1× in 2018 (FFAJ data, as cited by Hayo & Iwatsubo, 2019).
- **Behaviour (BOJ).**
  - Retail traders are contrarian at holding periods of a day or more. Below a day they are mostly contrarian, sometimes trend-following (2018).
  - Positions are mainly yen-short / foreign-currency-long, and forced loss-cuts amplify sharp yen rallies (2016).
  - Retail scalping spread as spreads narrowed (2016).
- **Interbank.** Algorithmic trading cut triangular arbitrage and the autocorrelation of high-frequency returns (Chaboud et al., 2014).
- **Implication.** Daily mean reversion in JPY crosses is already the crowd's default trade, and the professional side is algorithmic.

### 2.5 US stocks

- **HFT.** SEC staff (2014) cite estimates that HFT typically exceeded 50% of volume (2010 Concept Release). Carrion (2013) finds HFT on at least one side of 68.3% of dollar volume.
- **Retail routing.** More than 90% of individual investors' marketable orders are routed to six wholesalers (SEC release 2022-225).
- **Retail share of volume.** There is no official statistic; industry estimates are about 15–25% (low confidence).
- **Most-studied market.** Anomaly returns are 26% lower out of sample and 58% lower after publication (McLean & Pontiff, 2016). Anomaly returns roughly halved after decimalization (Chordia, Subrahmanyam & Tong, 2014).

## 3. Documented short-horizon predictability

All samples below end in 2019 or earlier.

### 3.1 Japanese equities

| Finding | Horizon | Sample | Cost / decay note | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Momentum everywhere except Japan | 12-1 months | Nov 1990–Mar 2011 | n/a | Fama & French (2012) |
| Significant 1-month reversal; contrarian works at about 1 month or beyond 2 years, unlike in the US and Europe | 1 month | TSE 1975–1997 | n/a | Iihara, Kato & Tokunaga (2004) and Chou, Wei & Chung (2007), via the Sasaki & Miyazaki (2012) review |
| Weekly reversal comes from the prior week's intraday returns, not overnight returns. It is stronger in illiquid stocks and volatile markets, and reflects price concessions to liquidity providers. Reported for US, Japan, UK and Eurozone | 1 week | Multi-country | You harvest it by providing liquidity, so it is sensitive to costs | Miwa (2019) |
| Conditioning on turnover: high-turnover stocks show 1-month momentum (positive in all 22 markets including Japan; 1.39%/month, t 3.65); low-turnover stocks reverse (−3.25%/month); plain value-weighted reversal is weak (−0.37%/month, t −1.29) | 1 month | 22 developed markets, 1993–2018 | Survives costs in the US | Medhat & Schmeling (2022) |
| A CNN trained on US 5-day OHLC/volume images, applied to Japan without retraining: annualised long-short Sharpe 5.84 equal-weight and 1.30 value-weight (local retraining gives 3.56 / 0.96) | 1 week | About 3,056 stocks/month, 1993–2019 | Gross of costs. Equal-weight far above value-weight means the effect is concentrated in small caps | Jiang, Kelly & Xiu (2023), Table X |
| Market-level intraday momentum is mainly evident in China and Japan | Intraday | APAC | Contested by HFTs | Limkriangkrai, Chai & Zheng (2023) |
| No reliable decay after publication outside the US | n/a | 241 anomalies, 39 markets | Japanese anomalies are less arbitraged | Jacobs & Müller (2020) |

### 3.2 Index futures

| Finding | Horizon | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Time-series momentum in all 58 futures: returns persist 1–12 months, then partly reverse | Monthly | Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen (2012) |
| Little asset-by-asset evidence; the pooled t-statistic is unreliable; the strategy performs about like a historical-mean strategy | Monthly | Huang, Li, Wang & Zhou (2020) |
| Intraday time-series momentum in most of 16 developed markets; stronger when liquidity is low, volatility high and news discrete | Intraday | Li, Sakkas & Urquhart (2022) |
| Japanese index futures' next-day intraday returns reverse the prior day's S&P 500 return (needs US data, so not a single-series candle signal) | Next day | Iwanaga (2023) |
| Volatility scaling raises Sharpe for equities and credit (leverage effect) and cuts extreme returns across 60+ assets | Daily scaling | Harvey et al. (2018) |
| Out-of-sample volatility management of 103 equity strategies usually fails to beat the unmanaged versions | Monthly | Cederburg et al. (2020) |

### 3.3 FX

- **Rossi (2013).** The random walk without drift is the toughest forecasting benchmark.
- **Neely, Weller & Ulrich (2009).** Filter and moving-average rule profits were genuine in the 1970s and 1980s but had disappeared by the early 1990s.
- **Hsu, Taylor & Wang (2016).** Some technical predictability survives a data-snooping control, but it varies by period and region and is tied to market immaturity.
- **Menkhoff et al. (2012).** Cross-sectional currency momentum reaches up to 10% a year, partly explained by transaction costs, with effective limits to arbitrage.
- **Harvey et al. (2018).** Volatility scaling has a negligible Sharpe effect for currencies.
- **Andersen et al. (2003) and Corsi (2009).** FX realised volatility is highly forecastable with simple models, which makes HAR-type models hard baselines.

### 3.4 US

- **Jiang, Kelly & Xiu (2023): headline result.** Weekly long-short Sharpe is 7.15 equal-weight and 1.49 value-weight, gross, at about 690% monthly turnover.
- **Jiang, Kelly & Xiu (2023): 500 largest stocks.** Equal-weight long-short earns 0.12%/week (Sharpe 1.02) at 712% monthly turnover. The authors say the weekly strategy is "mostly accessible to investors who behave as market makers".
- **Jiang, Kelly & Xiu (2023): after costs and over longer horizons.** At 10/20 bp costs the net weekly equal-weight Sharpe reaches 4.0 in the full universe. At longer horizons the edge sits in the long leg.
- **Avramov, Cheng & Metzker (2023).** Machine-learning profits come from hard-to-arbitrage stocks and fall further after costs.
- **Nagel (2012).** Reversal returns are the returns to liquidity provision and are predictable with the VIX.
- **de Groot, Huij & Zhou (2012).** Reversal earns 30–50 bp/week net in large caps with turnover control.
- **Brogaard, Hendershott & Riordan (2014).** HFTs trade against transitory pricing errors, which removes intraday predictability.

## 4. Can a weak signal survive costs? My arithmetic, with assumptions stated

### 4.1 Weekly cost hurdle

Assumption: turnover like Jiang, Kelly & Xiu's 500 largest stocks, 712% per month, which is about 1.78× the book per week per leg. Weekly cost = 1.78 × one-way cost.

| One-way cost case | One-way cost | Weekly cost, long-only | Weekly cost, long-short |
|---|---|---|---|

### 4.2 Breadth and power

- **Fundamental law.** IR ≈ IC × √breadth (Grinold, 1989), multiplied by a transfer coefficient below 1 under constraints such as long-only and lot sizes (Clarke, de Silva & Thorley, 2002).
- **Single instrument.** At IC 0.02 with a 12-day horizon (about 21 independent bets a year), IR ≈ 0.09 gross. With daily bets, IR ≈ 0.32 gross.
- **Power.** Reaching t = 3 at IC 0.02 needs about 22,500 independent observations, roughly 90 years of daily data on one instrument. Single-instrument direction (futures, FX) is therefore untestable, not merely weak.
- **Cross-section in the dev window.** With about 460 dev-window days and overlap-adjusted Newey-West, t ≥ 3 at IC 0.02 needs the standard deviation of daily IC to be at most 0.041 at a 12-day horizon, 0.064 at 5 days, or 0.14 at 1 day.
- **Noise floor.** Rank-IC sampling noise alone is about 1/√N ≈ 0.025 at N ≈ 1,600 stocks.
- **Comparison with #375.** That test found IC 0.022 at t 1.39 (user note); reaching t = 3 at the same dispersion would need about 4.7× more effective data.
- **What this means for pre-registration.** A 5-day variant has more power than the 12-day setting. Alternatively, accept that a pass requires an IC of roughly 0.04 or more.

### 4.3 Sizing granularity

- **TSE.** Stocks trade in 100-share units (JPX, since 2018). At an illustrative ¥2,000 price, one lot is ¥200,000, or 40% of ¥500k. That allows about 2–5 names at ¥500k and 15–30 at ¥3M.
- **OSE Micro.** One contract is the index × ¥10, which is ¥300,000 at JPX's 30,000 example. That is 60% of ¥0.5M, 30% of ¥1M or 10% of ¥3M per contract. Volatility targeting is coarse below ¥1–3M.

## 5. Horizon

- **Intraday.** HFTs account for 80–99% of order messages and 40–65% of executions. The documented intraday momentum is market-level and contested by HFTs. Intraday is also outside the daily Kronos setting. Avoid.
- **1-day.** Reversal here is a liquidity-provision premium (Nagel; Miwa) that turns over about 100% of the book per day. Direction has the power problem from Section 4.2. Avoid, except as a high-power diagnostic of IC.
- **5–12 days.** Jiang, Kelly & Xiu find candle signals most potent in the first week and still significant on days 6–20. Japan's weekly reversal is documented. Kronos's 12-bar horizon fits here. This is the recommended zone for ranking.
- **Monthly and longer.** This is the horizon of the time-series momentum literature for futures and FX, and the only one at which US access costs could be absorbed. It lies beyond Kronos's 12-bar forecast.

## 6. Which Kronos use fits each market

| Market | Cross-sectional ranking | Single-instrument direction | Volatility forecast for sizing |
|---|---|---|---|
| TSE stocks | **Best fit**: thousands of names, documented reversal and candle predictability. Needs a liquidity filter and capital for breadth | n/a | Secondary: position sizing across names, limited by lot size |
| TSE ETFs | Weak: tens of instruments and low breadth | Same weakness as futures, without leverage | Possible for an index ETF |
| OSE futures | n/a (four or fewer correlated contracts) | Weak and untestable at IC ≈ 0.02 | **Best fit**: volatility scaling helps equity indices (Harvey 2018); Micro contracts allow sizing at ¥1–3M |
| FX | Possible across pairs, but effective breadth is small (shared USD and JPY legs) and currency momentum faces limits to arbitrage | **Weakest** | Risk control only (no Sharpe gain for FX); HAR and GARCH are strong baselines |
| US stocks | Largest breadth and strongest gross evidence, but viable only at monthly, low-turnover settings given 0.495% per side | n/a | Possible |

Code facts from Kronos at pinned commit 67b630e, model/kronos.py:
- **Inputs (L489–491, L528–530).** Inputs are open, high, low, close, volume and amount. Missing volume is filled with zeros, so an FX feed without volume gives the model no volume information.
- **Normalisation (L544–547, L556).** Each window is z-normalised per column using its own mean and standard deviation, then clipped to ±5, and forecasts are de-normalised afterwards. Cross-sectional ranks therefore reflect only the shape of each window, not levels such as size or liquidity. This is analogous to Jiang, Kelly & Xiu's per-image scaling, which they call a key component of image-based prediction.
- **Sample-path averaging (L465–467).** Sample paths are averaged inside the inference loop. P(up) and dispersion therefore need per-path outputs, which the pre-registration already plans.

conclusions: Most likely to keep a candle-only edge after costs: TSE single stocks. Use cross-sectional ranking at a 5–12 trading-day horizon, restricted to liquid TOPIX500-type names, long-only or long-biased. The evidence: momentum is absent in Japan; 1-month and weekly reversal is documented; the US-trained candle CNN transfers to Japan (gross weekly long-short Sharpe 5.84 equal-weight, 1.30 value-weight); and anomalies show no reliable decay after publication outside the US. One tick costs about 1–5 bp in TOPIX500 names. The binding constraint is breadth under 100-share lots at ¥500k.

Second: OSE Nikkei 225 Micro or mini-TOPIX futures, with Kronos used only for volatility forecasts that size a fixed exposure. Volatility scaling raises Sharpe for equity indices (Harvey et al. 2018) and costs about 2.4 bp per round trip. Direction is HFT- and foreigner-dominated and untestable at IC ≈ 0.02. One Micro contract is about 60% of ¥500k at JPX's 30,000 example, so sizing is coarse below ¥1–3M.

US stocks have the strongest gross candle predictability but the most competition: HFT above 50% of volume, more than 90% of retail marketable orders internalised, and anomaly returns 58% lower after publication. Access costs from Japan are the highest (0.495% per side). The weekly large-cap spread (12 bp gross) is below even a 10 bp institutional cost. Only monthly, low-turnover ranking could plausibly survive.

Least likely: single-instrument FX direction. The random walk is the hardest benchmark; technical-rule profits in major currencies had disappeared by the early 1990s; the interbank market is algorithmic; Japanese retail traders, the largest retail FX pool, are already contrarian at ≥1-day horizons; Kronos receives zero volume for FX; and volatility targeting adds no Sharpe for currencies. Kronos in FX is at most a risk-control tool.

Horizon: avoid intraday (HFTs place 80–99% of order messages; it is also outside the daily setting) and 1-day (a liquidity-provision premium at about 100% turnover per day). 5–12 days is the only zone that is workable for ranking. Monthly is the only horizon at which US access costs could be absorbed.

Statistical power is decisive. Single-instrument direction at IC 0.02 needs about 22,500 independent observations for t = 3, so the futures and FX direction tests cannot pass. Even cross-sectionally, in about 460 dev days a 12-day-horizon IC of 0.02 reaches Newey-West t ≥ 3 only if the standard deviation of daily IC is ≤ 0.041 (≤ 0.064 at 5 days). Consider a 5-day variant, or accept that a pass needs an IC of roughly 0.04 or more.

new_findings.finding: FSA Fig. 2-4 (Jan–Jun 2026, read from chart, ±2 pp) gives HFT shares of trading value by product. Nikkei 225 Micro ≈72% and mini-TOPIX ≈78% are the highest among the major index futures. Nikkei 225 mini ≈62%, Nikkei 225 Futures ≈47%, JPX-Nikkei 400 ≈45%, TOPIX Futures ≈42%, Growth 250 ≈36%, long JGB futures ≈32%. JPX 2025 data show Micro proprietary at 0.0% and foreigners at 69.3%, consistent with HFT flow being booked as foreign brokerage.
new_findings.impact: Rank-2's instruments (Micro and mini-TOPIX) are the most HFT-dominated OSE index futures. That rules out any intraday or short-horizon directional use. For a daily volatility-sizing overlay it mainly implies tight market-maker spreads, which helps costs.

new_findings.finding: In Medhat & Schmeling, Japan's 1-month effect depends on turnover. Fig. 3 (value-weighted, 1993–2018) shows Japan's short-term momentum (high turnover) at Sharpe ≈ +0.4 and its reversal (low turnover) at Sharpe ≈ −1.5. Internationally, short-term momentum rises with size: top size quintile 1.12%/mo (t 4.01); value-weighted largest-100-per-country 0.62%/mo (t 3.25).
new_findings.impact: In liquid, high-turnover TOPIX500 names, which are the cheap ones to trade, the 1-month reversal is weakest and continuation may dominate. Rank-1's 'Japan = reversal' premise needs a turnover-conditional check before pre-registration.

new_findings.finding: Interactive Brokers Securities Japan (FSA-registered, 関東財務局(金商)第187号, JSDA member, has an API) charges for US stocks: Tiered USD 0.0035/share (min USD 0.35/order); Fixed USD 0.005/share (min USD 1.00); maximum 1% of trade value. Currency conversion is 0.20 bp, minimum USD 2.00.
new_findings.impact: US per-side cost is about 1–6 bp instead of 49.5 bp, so the 88 bp/week hurdle in EDGE-56 does not hold at this broker. Rank-3 ('US only as monthly low-turnover ranking') then rests on competition and statistical-power arguments, not on cost.

new_findings.finding: Derived from EDGE-55: with a TOPIX500-sized universe (N≈500), the daily rank-IC sampling noise alone is ≈1/√499 ≈ 0.045. That exceeds the 0.041 SD threshold for NW t≥3 at a 12-day horizon over ≈446 TSE days (t ≈ 2.7 even with zero common-factor noise). At 5 days the threshold is 0.063, which leaves little margin once factor noise is added.
new_findings.impact: Rank-1 (TOPIX500-type, 5–12 days) cannot reach t≥3 at IC 0.02 in the dev window by construction. Options: widen N (Prime ~1,600, at higher costs), use 5-day horizons, or pre-register a lower evidence bar or a longer window.
new_findings.source: Derived from EDGE-55 inputs and the JPX dev-window trading-day count

new_findings.finding: 三菱UFJ eスマート証券 (kabuステーション API provider) charges no domestic-stock commission at any trade value when an SOR order is selected; Nagoya, Fukuoka and Sapporo listings are excluded. Whether SOR orders can be sent through the API was not verified.
new_findings.impact: Supports EDGE-56's zero-commission premise for TOPIX500 names, provided the API supports SOR routing. Routing to PTS venues also changes fills and closing-price assumptions.

new_findings.finding: FSA Fig. 1-2-2 (TSE value by server location): the non-colocated 'other' share fell from ~52–57% (2025) to ~43–44% (Jan–Jun 2026). The colocated non-HFT share rose from ~9–13% to ~16–19%, and colocated HFT rose to 38% by Jun 2026.
new_findings.impact: Algorithmic competition in TSE cash equities rose during the dev and holdout windows. This argues against short-horizon edges in large caps; market structure only, no price data used.

new_findings.finding: Per-product HFT share of OSE trading value, Jan–Jun 2026 (FSA Fig. 2-4, read from a bar chart, ±2pp): Nikkei 225 Micro ≈72%, mini-TOPIX ≈78%, Nikkei 225 mini ≈62%, Nikkei 225 Futures ≈47%, TOPIX Futures ≈42%, JPX-Nikkei 400 ≈45%, Growth 250 ≈36%. On OSE, HFTs place about 100% of FAK orders and about 0% of market orders (p.12).
new_findings.impact: The two contracts proposed for rank (2) are the most HFT-dominated index futures on OSE. Any use for direction or intraday trading is head-to-head with HFT. Using them only for daily volatility sizing remains coherent, but this rules out a directional variant.

new_findings.finding: Plain short-term reversal is gone or negative in large liquid stocks in modern data. JKX Table IV (US top 500, 2001–2019 test): STR/R5 −0.02%/wk (Sharpe −0.11) and WSTR/R5 −0.05%/wk equal-weight; value-weight −0.02 and −0.04. Novy-Marx & Velikov (VW deciles on NYSE breakpoints, 1963–2012): short-run reversal earns 0.37%/month gross (t 1.71) at 91% monthly turnover with costs of 1.65%/month, so net −1.28%/month (t −6.02). Avramov, Chordia & Goyal (2006): reversal profits sit in high-turnover, low-liquidity stocks and 'are smaller than the likely transactions costs'.
new_findings.impact: The Japan reversal literature (equal-weight, small caps, samples ending 1990–1997, gross) does not support a TOPIX500 strategy. Any edge in liquid names would have to come from non-reversal patterns (the CNN's top-500 Sharpe of about 1.0 gross at about 710% monthly turnover), which weakens the 'Japan reversal' case for rank (1).
new_findings.source: JKX JF 2023 Table IV (https://economics.yale.edu/sites/default/files/2023-11/The%20Journal%20of%20Finance%20-%202023%20-%20JIANG%20-%20Re%25E2%2580%2590%20Imag%20in%20ing%20Price%20Trends_0.pdf); https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w20721/w20721.pdf Table 3 Panel C; https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/jfinan/v61y2006i5p2365-2394.html

new_findings.finding: Medhat & Schmeling cost table (US, 1983–2018 half-spreads): reversal among low-turnover stocks (STREV*) earns 1.41%/month gross against 1.94%/month in half-spread costs, so it loses money net. Short-term momentum among large caps nets 0.62%/month (t 3.14). Internationally (22 developed markets including Japan, 1993–2018), value-weight STMOM on the 100 largest stocks per country earns 0.62%/month (t 3.25), and conventional value-weight STREV is not significant (t −1.29).
new_findings.impact: In liquid TOPIX500-type names the 1-month sign may be momentum, not reversal, and the reversal that does exist (illiquid names) is eaten by spreads. A candle model's learned 'buy the recent loser' prior is risky in exactly the universe chosen for low costs.

new_findings.finding: The Japanese short-term contrarian profit comes mainly from lead-lag effects (cross-autocorrelation of firm-specific components) per Chou, Wei & Chung (2007, JEF 14(3)). Miwa (2019) and Nagel (2012) describe reversal as a liquidity-provision premium: larger in illiquid stocks and high-VIX states, small in calm periods. An excerpt of Chang, McLeavey & Rhee (1995, JBFA; TSE 1975–1991) says net-of-cost short-term contrarian profits were justified 'only for brokers'; low confidence, because the PDF could not be opened (TLS error). No post-2010 (arrowhead/HFT era) Japan-specific net-of-cost reversal study was found; status unknown.
new_findings.impact: A daily-bar retail strategy that takes liquidity pays this premium rather than earning it. On the TSE, market making is about 15% of HFT value and HFTs place about 80% of new orders. The premium is likely concentrated in names and periods a ¥0.5–3M long-only book cannot exploit.

new_findings.finding: Chen & Velikov (2023, JFQA 58(3)): after effective spreads, post-publication decay and the modern trading-technology era since the early 2000s, the average of 204 US anomalies earns 'a measly 4 bps per month'. The strongest earn at best about 10 bp after controlling for data mining, and combinations earn about 20 bp, all before price impact.
new_findings.impact: This sets a near-zero base rate for a public price-based signal surviving costs. 'No reliable post-publication decay outside the US' (Jacobs & Müller) does not establish net profitability today, and no Japan-specific equivalent of Chen & Velikov was found.

new_findings.finding: 'Momentum is absent in Japan' is weak as a structural premise. Fama & French (2012) call it plausibly 'a chance result', and their equal-WML test across regions does not reject at 90%. Asness (2011, JPM 37(4), July 1981–Dec 2010, top 90% of market cap, VW): Japan's momentum Sharpe is 0.03, but with eight value/momentum strategies at a true Sharpe of 0.35, the chance that at least one comes in at 0.03 or below is 26%. Japan's momentum is strongly negatively correlated with value, and its three-factor intercepts are significantly positive.
new_findings.impact: The Japan-exception argument for ranking Japan first is mostly noise plus correlation with value. It should not carry weight in market selection.

new_findings.finding: Statistical power in the chosen universe: in a TOPIX500-type universe (N ≈ 500) the rank-IC sampling floor 1/√N ≈ 0.045 already exceeds the 0.041 std(IC) ceiling needed for t ≥ 3 at IC 0.02, h = 12, over 460 days. Qian & Hua (2004) find realised std(IC) averages about 1.5× that floor (range about 1.0–2.6×, 60 strategies, Russell 3000, 1987–2003).
new_findings.impact: Rank (1)'s universe (TOPIX500) and its 12-day horizon conflict with what the pre-registration can detect. Either pre-register h = 5 (feasible only if κ ≲ 1.4) or a broader universe (N ≈ 1,600, at higher spread costs), or accept that a 12-day TOPIX500 test can only find IC ≥ 0.03.

new_findings.finding: Interactive Brokers Securities Japan is an FSA-registered Japanese entity of a foreign broker (関東財務局長（金商）第187号, JSDA member). It lists an API and charges for US stocks $0.005/share Fixed (minimum $1.00 per order, maximum 1% of value) or $0.0005–0.0035/share Tiered (minimum $0.35 plus exchange and clearing fees). Pricing page fetched 2026-11-08 and may change.
new_findings.impact: The US per-side cost is about 4–20 bp for small orders, not 49.5 bp, so rank (3) (monthly US ranking) becomes materially cheaper. The weekly US verdict still holds, because roughly 8 bp/week gross long-only excess in JKX's top 500 does not cover the cost.

new_findings.finding: Volatility timing of the market has a weak out-of-sample record. Liu, Tang & Zhou (2019, JPM 46(1) 38–51): Moreira-Muir-style vol timing uses a look-ahead scaling constant; once corrected, maximum drawdowns are 68–93% and it beats the market only in the financial crisis, and three alternative timing strategies also fail. Harvey et al. (2018): for equity index futures, simple EWMA scaling improves Sharpe only 'slightly'; the robust benefit is lower tail risk. Cederburg et al. (2020): no systematic out-of-sample gain across 103 strategies.
new_findings.impact: Rank (2)'s upside is second-order. A Kronos volatility forecast must beat EWMA/HAR (EDGE-46) just to match a gain that is itself slight. Expect a risk-control tool, not an edge, and pre-register an EWMA/HAR baseline.

new_findings.finding: Hsu & Kuan (2005, JFEc 3(4)), using White's Reality Check and Hansen's SPA test to control data snooping: technical rules are significantly profitable only in 'young' markets (NASDAQ Composite, Russell 2000), not in mature ones (DJIA, S&P 500), over roughly 1990–2003 (period from a secondary source). Park & Irwin (2007, JES 21(4)): technical profits across speculative markets held 'at least until the early 1990s'.
new_findings.impact: Candle-only direction on mature large-index futures (Nikkei 225/TOPIX) is the least promising use. This supports restricting OSE futures to sizing only.

new_findings.finding: JKX's international transfer results rest on Datastream daily data. Ince & Porter (2006, JFR 29(4) 463–479) document Datastream individual-equity return data problems that require screening. In JKX, Japan's value-weight transfer gain is significant only at 10% (+0.34*), and transfer fails in the UK (−0.10 EW), India (−1.30) and China (−2.30).
new_findings.impact: The Japan 5.84 equal-weight figure is gross, driven by small and illiquid stocks, and possibly sensitive to data errors. The 1.30 value-weight figure (gross, weekly, about 700%+ monthly turnover, 'market-maker' territory) is the relevant one for a liquid-names plan.

new_findings.finding: TSE's own tick-reform documents (2026) define the 'appropriate' quoted spread as 1.5–5.0 ticks (STR). From 2027-03-01, tables A/B/C are reassigned every August from the median daily STR over August–April. Stocks with STR below 1.5 move to finer ticks; stocks above 5.0 move to coarser ticks.
new_findings.impact: A 1-tick spread on TOPIX500 names is a best case; the actual distribution of spreads is unknown because no per-stock statistics were found. The tick and cost regime will change during any forward test after 2027-03 and again every August, so cost assumptions must be re-estimated per regime.

new_findings.finding: US evidence (SEC staff review) is that HFTs are 'much more active in large-cap stocks' (Brogaard, Hendershott & Riordan; large caps are 96% of dollar volume in their sample). The FSA report gives no size breakdown of TSE HFT share; the Japan figure is unknown.
new_findings.impact: By analogy, the TOPIX500 names chosen because they are cheap to trade are probably where HFT participation is above the market-wide high-30s%. Low cost and low competition pull in opposite directions.

new_findings.finding: In weekly TSE data (2008–2016), the cumulative market-timing performance of domestic investor groups (the contrarian side) is 'overwhelmed by foreign investors', who are the trend-chasing side.
new_findings.impact: At the aggregate level, the contrarian crowd a reversal strategy would join lost to the 66%-of-value foreign flow. This is weak but contrary evidence to framing retail contrarians as harvestable or as a reason Japan rewards reversal. It concerns aggregate market timing, not cross-sectional selection.

new_findings.finding: Kronos code at 67b630e: predict() defaults to sample_count=1 (L519). With more samples, paths are averaged before return (L465–467), so the forecast distribution's spread is never exposed. Scaling uses the lookback window's price-level mean and std (L544, L556), so the forecast scale is anchored to the 40-bar window.
new_findings.impact: Rank (2) needs repeated single-sample calls or a code patch, and a range-based (high–low) volatility read-out. Its built-in anchor is close to a 40-day rolling estimate, so beating EWMA/HAR is the binding test, not an afterthought.
